Advancements in deep learning, spurred by substantial educational datasets like the Medicare and Cancer educations, have driven innovations in educational systems. Nevertheless, existing studies predominantly centered on a single form of data, utilizing either medical images or text-based information from electronic health records to educate users. This limitation severely hampers the potential of educational systems, given the richness and diversity of other modalities like biomedical images or signals. To address this shortcoming, we have developed a pioneering approach that integrates multiple modalities to create various educational systems. Our methodology begins with harvesting knowledge from extensive cancer databases to create knowledge graphs concerning non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) prognosis. By structuring this knowledge into graph domains and range, our education system is empowered to utilize any combination of existing knowledge nodes as a teaching framework. To facilitate effective education, we employ graph neural networks in conjunction with relevant modalities like medical images or signals, subject matter expert knowledge, and educational goals to adapt the knowledge framework. Our educational method is versatile, accommodating various teaching styles by iterating over different graph nodes and domain ranges. Through explicit training on selected educational goals, our system is capable of adjusting the knowledge framework to suit individual learners and achieve customized educational objectives. Ultimately, we have demonstrated the potential of our educational method by comparing its effectiveness on prognosis prediction using cancer databases containing multiple modalities.

A well-defined environment is crucial in the process of reinforcement learning, particularly when employing artificial agents in real-life scenarios. Unlike static settings, authentic environments are characterized by unpredictable changes in both state and action results. Moreover, authentic environments are often interpreted as complex, state-dependent Markov Decision Processes, even though the dynamics and models behind them are not publicly accessible. Authentic environment modeling has significant implications in reinforcement learning, particularly during training, where artificial agents interact with their surroundings. This paper delves into the topic of authentic environment learning from both theoretical and practical perspectives, before discussing existing methods and assessing their merits. Additionally, we highlight existing challenges and propose potential avenues for further investigation.

A novel approach to determining the energy spectrum of intergalactic gas is presented, leveraging a deep learning model trained with synthetic spectra generated through cosmological simulations. These synthetic spectra were created utilizing two sets of simulations based on two distinct cosmological models, both incorporating Omega_m = 0.31 and Omega_L = 0.69. By achieving high accuracy in predicting the spectrum of new, unseen quasars, our model effectively grasps complex relationships within the synthetic spectra. When extrapolating to redshifts exceeding 6, our results demonstrate reasonable agreement with existing observations. Additionally, our methodology enables estimates of the hydrogen absorption spectrum and allows for the comparison of these predictions with actual observations, yielding compatible values for key spectral features. Moreover, our model can reproduce the spectrum of a specific quasar, including noise, with low error, particularly at high frequency frequencies.

This article delves into the characteristics of U(∅)-vacant modules in the context of Lie algebras of derivative operators, where U(∅) represents the universal enveloping algebra derived from the Lie algebra of derivative operators. Additionally, we investigate the Lie algebra of first derivative operators and its homologous Lie bialgebra.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. Our
objective is to identify the most effective method for classifying short, informal text
exhibiting subjective language. Our analysis involves comparing various pre-trained
models, word embeddings, and neural network architectures, such as RoBERT and RoBERTa, in
the context of LSTM. Our findings indicate that an LSTM model leverages word embeddings
and includes a dropout rate of 0.15 performs better than 96% of baseline classifications.

Recently, various chatbots based on large language models have been popular 
opposite ends of the spectrum from traditional custom-built systems, with 
general-purpose models or ones with added custom features. Our system aims to
fill a gap by providing a versatile platform that can easily incorporate
specialized roles to enhance various conversational interactions. To achieve
this, we utilize the Llama model and define specific conversation roles to
handle common queries, incorporating essential knowledge and applicable rules
derived from relevant studies. By establishing clear guidelines and a user
classification system, our role-defined open-domain conversation system can
effortlessly incorporate new features to ensure consistent and meaningful
conversation flows.

The explosion of supernovae and the collapse of massive stars in distant galaxies may create a random backdrop of gravitational waves in our daily lives, caused by the temporary disturbance known as gravitational wave memory. Researchers have found that the intensity of these background signals is significantly weaker than the static noise in radio waves, making their current detection by Earth-based instruments impossible. However, the signals' immense scale, stemming from the vast distances of galaxies, could potentially be measured using highly advanced detectors capable of pinpointing extremely faint signals, and could serve as a means of verifying the existence of gravitational wave memory and exploring its underlying theoretical framework.

A hypothetical state of matter is proposed to explain several observed phenomena, including extremely rare nuclear interactions, vast cosmic radiation, and the heavy elements in the universe. This state of matter is thought to stem from a change within a fundamental physical system, characterized by broken supersymmetry, a significantly displaced fermion spectrum, and extremely massive spin-zero particles. It is postulated that this state of matter is comprised of pure gauge bosons, while a different sector of particles is responsible for the phenomenon of neutrino mass generation. Calculations indicate that the amounts of neutrino mass and heavy element production are compatible with existing data. Furthermore, this theory predicts the presence of cosmic-scale black holes, of order $10^{18-20}$ grams, created via the collapse of early universe matter. These black holes would have an extremely high rate of merger events audible to our current gravitational wave detectors. Ultimately, the theory forecasts a vast, dense cosmic environment where ordinary matter exists as a minor minority.

A reliable and efficient communication infrastructure is crucial for every-day life and many industrial applications. Researchers were able to endow semantic communications with the ability to efficiently and securely transmit information by utilizing complex reward functions. However, these reward functions require substantial knowledge of the environment and are difficult to apply in real-world scenarios. To overcome these challenges, a novel approach combines causal inference and the signaling game to create a flexible and efficient environment for semantic communications. By using a data-driven and symbolic representation of the environment, the communication system can learn to transmit semantically enriched data that adheres to complex constraints and increases overall system efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves the information transfer rate by 213% and reduces errors by 97% compared to conventional methods.

In information retrieval, term prediction plays a crucial role in enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of search engines and knowledge bases. This research proposes a new hybrid framework that integrates Naive Bayes and Latent Knowledge for term prediction, leveraging document categories and term co-occurrence patterns to identify missing search query terms. The proposed model addresses the limitations of previous approaches by incorporating document categories, improving modeling, and enhancing flexibility through adaptive knowledge. Furthermore, this framework can be applied beyond search query term suggestion, also enabling semantic enrichment of individual documents and knowledge articles.

Recent sessions-based recommendation systems have gained popularity due to their robust performance in real-world settings, particularly when users' browsing history is extensive. These systems excel at providing relevant suggestions as users navigate through content, with numerous session-based models proposed in the literature. However, high-quality suggestions are greatly dependent on the quality of suggestion lists provided at each stage of the session. Unfortunately, existing models have an inherent limitation in their suggestion lists - they lack flexibility and are often insufficient for guiding users' exploration. This is because current lists are typically one-dimensional, presenting items in a straight line, which fails to accurately reflect users' diverse interests and preferences. In contrast, vertical layouts are not suitable for presentation, and ratings or rankings are often difficult to convey in a list format. To address this, we introduce a new session-based recommendation framework that provides two-phase suggestions, incorporating a learning component to derive user representations and another for discovering relevant items. Additionally, our framework involves learning candidate rank representations to better model users' preferences and the relative merits of suggested items, which are then utilized in a joint training approach with existing rank learning methods. Ultimately, our approach leads to enhanced suggestion lists that are more adept at guiding users' exploration and presenting relevant content.

In a surroundings where particles exhibit varying levels of activity, a theoretical framework suggests that particles move towards areas with optimal levels of activity, where their velocity matches their mobility. This study demonstrates that this behavior results from a balance between active propulsion and the particle's size, leading to a reduction in velocity beyond a certain critical activity threshold. Furthermore, we examine the particle's dynamics when exposed to activity fluctuations and show that, although small fluctuations have minimal impact, significant fluctuations can cause the particle to change its direction. Moreover, we propose that certain fluctuations can propel the particle to previously inaccessible areas behind the particle. Additionally, we investigate the effect of Verwey-Overbeek interactions between colloidal particles and show that this interaction can alter the particle's trajectory.

This research develops a novel numerical approach for modeling three-dimensional fluid flow through discrete fractures in porous media. Our methodology utilizes a coherent mesh consisting of a fractured domain and its surrounding porous media. We employ the mimetic finite difference method to formulate governing equations for fluid dynamics, incorporating fracture flow submodels. These submodels utilize respective formulas such as cubic law for fracture flow and cubic law with fracture entry resistance. We develop an iterative solution method to resolve pressure and saturation in the fractured porous media. Furthermore, our numerical approach is validated through various numerical experiments that demonstrate its accuracy and reliability.

Cellular structures pose a challenge for robotic navigation due to their intricate design and potential collision points. To address this issue, a new approach leverages point set registration to enable a swarm of drones to safely explore and document cellular structures while preserving their underlying geometry. This method relies on treating cells as rigid entities and using centroid-based alignment to minimize point set disruption and improve registration accuracy. Results from both simulated and real-world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in preserving cellular structure and avoiding collisions as the drones move through the structure.

This research delves into the properties of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, examining its eigenvalues, spectral radius, stable range of the Seidel matrix, and the Seidel energy of the graph.

This research investigates a parameter optimization problem for stochastic differential equations driven by a fractional Brownian motion, subject to constraints. The cost function is calculated based on the trajectories' mean path cost and their average distance from target points, all within a fixed time frame. The optimization goal is to minimize this cost. Theoretical justifications are established using tools from Borel and Lyapunov functions, and the proof shows that the mean path cost can be minimized while the average distance term can be made small enough. The results are applied to the regulation of fractional Brownian motion, and a numerical example illustrates the approach's effectiveness.

We've developed a new theory of elliptic finite-band energies for the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator. This involves constructing a non-self-adjoint, elliptic finite-band Dirac operator on a bounded domain in n-dimensional space and establishing the existence of elliptic finite-band Dirac eigenvalues. Furthermore, we've shown that these eigenvalues form a countable, unbounded set. This research generalizes the work of Shatah, Zwanzig, and Kapitanski on the projective metric on invariant subspaces of the Dirac operator.

Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on their surroundings, which can be perceived through their onboard cameras, sensors, and radars. Nevertheless, these devices often fall short in their perception due to obstacles such as trees, buildings, and weather conditions. To overcome these limitations, a two-tier network architecture has been proposed, which utilizes roadside units and vehicle relays to enhance auto-sensing capabilities. In the ensuing research, an analytical model is developed to quantify the gain in accuracy that vehicular networks can offer compared to auto-sensing systems. A simulation experiment was conducted using a simulation platform called Veins, which simulates the vehicular network within a designated area, to calculate the average field of view for both auto-sensing and 2-tier networks. The simulation results indicate that vehicular networks can provide a significant boost in coverage on urban roads, which could potentially improve safety features and reliability. A statistical analysis also showed that the shape of the field of view distribution is not uniform and can be modeled using a gamma distribution.

Wikipedia's an abundance of curated content stems from a massive volunteer force,
primarily untrained and unverified.  As a result, a small proportion of articles
demonstrates extremely poor quality, severely impacting reader experience and website
reputation.  Currently, detecting these flawed articles relies on manual, time-consuming
complementary inspections from both readers and editors.  Consequently, a substantial
amount of high-priority work on Wikipedia goes unaddressed.  To streamline the process,
we've developed a system that automatically flags low-quality articles, relying on patterns
in editing behaviors and machine learning algorithms.  Our method enables editors to prioritize
efforts on articles most in need.

One major issue with relying on user input in decision-based black-box explanations is the reliance on additional data, which can be difficult to obtain. Given the expense associated with gathering new data, it's often discarded or not collected at all. This paper explores the idea of applying explanations without requiring new data inputs. Without requiring user input, the approach utilizes existing information to create a predictive model, specifically on text data, utilizing an BERT* encoder and a simple transformer decoder to produce explanations in the format of "I can predict this way". The model is evaluated on various scenarios and is found to favor simplicity and clarity, and is capable of generating comparable results to a highly complex and trained baseline model. The associated code is available at https://github.com/jaysonbosson/Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay for the first time and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay. The observation and evidence came from an analysis of proton-proton collision data, 2011-2012, that were recorded by the CMS experiment at energies of 7 and 8 TeV and had a total luminosity of 65.1 inverse picobarns. The data were then compared to predicted theories, revealing that the branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ is approximately 1.11±0.24±0.13±0.01 per 10^4 particles and the branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ is around 1.77±0.26±0.08±0.02 per 10^4 particles.

We've developed a method to apply geometric T-duality on a variety of twisted torus configurations. Our method is versatile and allows various combinations of T-dual transformations, including both circle reductions and fiber expansions. We've demonstrated the computation of T-dual metrics through group backtracking and showed that this technique yields accurate results by comparing our calculations to known solutions for specific cases. Furthermore, we've illustrated the connection between geometric T-duality and the brane intersection philosophy by presenting examples of dual configurations.

In recent years, there has been an increased focus on Learning from Observations (LfO), which involves using data from expert sources to train entry-level professionals in observational skills. However, there are concerns about relying too heavily on from-scratch learning, which can be costly and time-consuming in real-world settings. On the other hand, fully pre-trained models may overlook essential details observed by experts and fail to incorporate essential expertise into their representations. To address these limitations, this research proposes the concept of co-observation learning (CoOl), which involves utilizing paired data from both the novice and expert to educate a model. By combining multiple features from both parties, CoOl overcomes the shortcomings of LfO and from-scratch learning, and demonstrates significant benefits over existing techniques through experiments conducted on public datasets.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using this metric, the polarization-adjusted convolutional code achieves superior error-correction performance and significantly lower decoding computations compared to the existing best-known polar codes. Specifically, at a low error probability, the code only requires computations relevant to the ARQ code, saving the bulk of computations needed for the polar codes. Furthermore, this optimized metric enables the direct calculation of ARQ codes, eliminating the need for decoding and error-checking operations. Experimental results confirm that the average computation savings of this optimized metric range from 60% to 90% compared to state-of-the-art polar codes, with minimal performance loss. Moreover, the optimized metric enables the direct calculation of ARQ codes with minimal performance loss.

A crucial capability for robots operating outdoors is the ability to grasp and manipulate everyday objects, and given the latest advancements in depth sensors, tracking hand movement is relatively straightforward. However, the major challenge remains in identifying and accounting for the intricate movements of the hands and objects within the complex outdoor environment. The main aim of our research is to develop a highly advanced, versatile system that can reconstruct interactions between the hands and objects in real-time, and we've successfully implemented this system in the context of widely available Reddy-Buxton datasets. The key techniques used here involve the rapid processing of multiple outdoor scenes, accurate 3D tracking of hands and objects, and the real-time planning and execution of hand movement trajectories. The effectiveness of our approach has been confirmed through quantitative analysis and user testing in the outdoors. The code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub.

This study completes the classification of a specific type of geometric group, known as the tail-triangle C-groups of grade 4, consisting of non-crystallographic Coxeter groups with a specific arrangement of mirrors. These groups have a unique growth pattern, and our classification adds to a broader understanding of a particular family of groups. Additionally, we have also compiled a comprehensive list of all non-crystallographic C-groups of grade 4 that possess a specific property, and our findings include cases with a unique local structure.

A significant challenge in using robots for food preparation and other applications has been addressed, namely the issue of calibrating the robot's perspective with a standard point of view. When working with unmarked objects, robots struggle to determine their position relative to the items they need to manipulate or interact with, let alone the focus of their vision. To overcome these obstacles, a novel method incorporates machine learning and statistics, leveraging depth data and object modeling to forecast key locations, which are then utilized to adjust the robot's viewpoint and accurately position its tools. This approach was tested with a DepthSense camera on a Universal Robots arm and validated through experiments involving various objects, revealing an average error margin of less than 3 centimeters.

In the context of targeted treatments, it's essential to evaluate how different strategies interact with one another in a given system. This paper delves into a specific framework, examining the effects of an untargeted treatment on a targeted treatment under specific conditions and develops a method to identify these interactions when certain assumptions are met. Within this framework, a key concept is how the treatment of an individual affects their neighbors, and to account for these complex relationships, the paper utilizes a model that breaks down these interactions into distinct sections. By breaking down these interactions into distinct sections, the paper is able to develop a specific model that best represents these complex relationships, and in doing so, identify specific factors that contribute to these interactions, providing new insights into how these interactions affect one another.

To estimate neutrino emissions from self-interacting dark matter within neutron stars, we simulated the process by randomly selecting 1 million points within a neutron star's cross-sectional area and connecting them with neighboring points based on their spatial relationship. This network allowed us to count 2.64 billion segments, with those that aren't directly connected (i.e., 'not straight line' segments) potentially producing additional neutrinos. By simulating the dark matter distribution within a neutron star, we found that 'not straight line' segments account for approximately 3.57% of all segments and that in models where interaction strength varies with distance, more particles produce 'not straight line' segments than in models with equal interactions towards all directions. Additionally, we calculated the ratio of newly produced neutrinos to existing ones and discovered that in certain interaction models, newly produced neutrinos could exceed existing ones within a neutron star. If this occurs, as evidenced by our chosen 1 TeV dm particle mass, it could happen at distances smaller than a few millimeters from the neutron star's surface. We observed that in certain cases, the new neutrinos could dominate existing ones by up to 100 times. If this phenomenon occurs, it could potentially explain the observed pulsar timing disruptions of certain neutron stars, altering the existing 'pulsar pair' model in which timing disruptions are primarily caused by existing neutrinos. The ongoing UNIONS/CFIS survey is conducting a comprehensive cosmological study over the large area of 8500 deg^2, employing a distinctive layout with 21 individual sub-projects. For shape measurement, the CoannisecTF pipeline, an optimized version of the ngmix code, is being utilized to analyze the survey's data. In this research, a new profile-based approach is introduced to measure galaxy shapes and applied to the CFIS data to obtain weak-lensing maps and critical density profiles. The study provides a foundation for future joint analyses of the CFIS and DES datasets.

A distinct set of real numbers $y_i$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, that satisfy $|y_j-y_k|>\frac{\pi}{2}$ for $j\neq k$, can be thought of as indices for functions $e(yi)t$, that range from $e(t)$ to $e(\tau t)$, where $\tau$ differs from $y_j-y_k$. When the set contains two or more elements, these functions are linearly independent. 

We investigate the distribution of numbers $y$ in the interval $[0,1)$ that, along with a given set of $n$ numbers $y_i$, where $i=1\ldots n$, cause the associated functions $e(yt)$ to achieve perfect accuracy at specific values of $t$, as dictated by a Novikov function $\Lambda(t)$, at both the continuous level and as part of a countable set $\Lambda(m)$ in the integers. 

It is established that, as the interval $y$ varies, the double set $(y,t)$ that satisfies $\Lambda(t)=0$ equally occupies the unit square in both a continuous sense and as part of a countable set $\mu(y)\geq\mathbb{E}[\Lambda(m)]_{L^{2}}(y,t)1_{\{t\in\Lambda^{-1}(0)\}}dydt$. 

This finding extends the initial Kenig-Wright result

We explore K-rational and K-Du Bois properties in conjunction with their respective implications on F-rational and F-Du Bois characteristics, with a focus on the local complete intersection case. Our analysis reveals that for a local complete intersection quasi-singular surface, K-rationality implies both F-rationality and F-Du Bois. Furthermore, our findings include an example illustrating the disparate nature of K-rational and F-rational properties and another example demonstrating the coexistence of K-rational with non-F-rational properties.

Researchers discovered that a magnetic material, which acts as a refined model for describing the behavior of superconducting materials, exhibits strong links between its internal magnetic fields and the movement of adjacent magnetic dipoles. By applying external magnetic fields, the materials transition from a highly ordered state at low temperatures to a more disordered state at higher temperatures, exhibiting increased fluctuations throughout the temperature range. This increased fluctuations phenomenon can be compared to the behavior of superconducting materials that are near a phase transition, where the same materials exhibit strong Correlated movements. Our research shows that these Correlated movements can be controlled by the external magnetic field and that this effect can be observed in the materials local heat distribution. This discovery opens up new possibilities for controlling the materials behavior and understanding the materials properties at the atomic level.

If the axion-dark matter hypothesis holds, we propose a thought experiment where an imaginary substance exists solely for theoretical purposes. Within this substance, neutrinos become sterile at a specific energy threshold. By leveraging the equation for heat capacity in relation to entropy, we explore the intrinsic properties of this substance, which exhibits anomalous behavior. Furthermore, we turn to quantum physics and statistical mechanics to outline the substance's quantum and classical attributes. Ultimately, we outline two distinct research paths that could verify the axion-dark matter hypothesis through the investigation of this substance's thermal characteristics.

Quantum computing applications often involve preparing and processing unique quantum states known as magic states, typically achieved through the use of noisy quantum adder circuits or quantum error correction codes. Notably, these states have considerable value despite existing outside the scope of classical descriptions. A crucial aspect is the search for the most efficient classical representations of magic states, measured in terms of the stabilizer rank - the minimum number of classical bits needed to describe a given state. Given the practical limitations of determining this rank directly, research has focused on establishing upper bounds through various proofs of stabilizer rank constraints. This study presents new proofs, leveraging previously unexplored properties of magic states to derive tighter upper limits on their stabilizer rank. Specifically, the article demonstrates that any 23-qubit Clifford+$\pi/14$ circuit can be realized within the first 21 qubits using a simplified, more robust approach, and that similar stability can be achieved with fewer than 0.4n qubits, based on a previous bound developed by Kuperberg. To establish these results, the authors developed novel spinor group embeddings and examined the effects of circulant permutations on spinor groups, introducing key properties and constraints in the process. Additionally, the article presents an alternative method for describing magic states using linear subspaces known as solvable spaces, and explores the potential connections between these spaces and quantum computing applications.

We investigate a Tsallis holographic dark energy model in a complex quintessence framework. By setting the sound horizon scale, we derive equations for the sound horizon and acoustical scale, and utilizing the property $\rho_f=-p_f/\kappa$, we establish the relationship between a complex scalar field and Tsallis holographic dark energy. Furthermore, we examine the influence of Tsallis parameter $q$ on the evolution of the universe, resulting in a transition from the current acceleration phase to a future slowdown or stop in acceleration phase, and ultimately to a Big Rip singularity.

Our initial investigation into the LAMOST's KD survey has yielded significant insights derived from four $K$2 differential space velocity project's initial 81,142 spectra. These spectra originated from astrophysical objects observed by the Gaia-2, -3, -4, and -5 fields, each containing multiple epochs. Our analysis involved verifying whether objects with multiple observations could detect variations within their H-alpha and Narrow-Line Region emission. After applying a measurement uncertainty limit and considering parallax uncertainty, we identified 13,673 stable objects with consistent spectra. Notably, 6,667 of these have detectable H-alpha variations, while 1,644 display H-alpha emission. Objects with H-alpha emission are predominantly found near the Gaia-2 and -3 fields, where they are more numerous than expected, despite Gaia's reported error margins suggesting lower counts. Additionally, we observed more narrow-line emission among red stars and within the Gaia-4 and -5 fields. These initial findings suggest that LAMOST's multi-timeframe monitoring, combined with LAMOST's spectral data, can complement Gaia's positional measurements to detect varied astrophysical phenomena.

We propose TuRaN, a genuine hardware-based RNG capable of generating high-quality, high-speed random numbers without relying on statistical post-processing techniques, thus eliminating the need for external sources and reducing energy consumption. By utilizing a section of SRAM memory and repeatedly switching between two adjacent voltage levels, TuRaN generates truly random numbers at a rate proportional to the memory access speed, thereby leveraging the inherent randomness caused by gasket leakage currents and considering both physical and physicality-related bias and robustness factors. The study includes detailed analysis, backed by extensive simulation results, demonstrating that TuRaN can maintain a high randomness quality even in the presence of varying process voltages and is resilient to various side-channel attacks affecting SRAM. For instance, a 32-entry SRAM-based TuRaN generator can produce 86.4 Mbps of high-quality random numbers while consuming 0.073 pJ per random number, thereby achieving a 10x energy efficiency improvement over leading hardware RNGs.

A fundamental concept underlying numerous novel technologies, including neuromorphic computing and spin-off technologies based on resistive random access memory, is the ability to swiftly switch individual atoms or molecules between high and low electrical conductivity states. Currently, there is significant debate about whether molecular single-electron resistive switches, which rely on electrostatic interactions with chargeable molecules, are feasible. To address this question, we have designed and studied two theoretical models of this type of switch, incorporating different types of noncrystallographic symmetry. Our research, however, found that both models exhibit unstable behavior which makes them impractical for practical use. To make progress in this field, we are encouraging the creation of artificial molecular environments that would make these switches stable and efficient in reality.

Feynman integrals are fundamental in Particle Physics, but their complex nature makes them difficult to evaluate exactly, prompting the development of innovative numerical and analytical approaches to resolve them. By applying the principles of effective field theories and exploiting symmetry, a causal representation of Feynman integrals can be achieved, facilitating both numerical and analytical evaluations. Causal Feynman integrals feature a clear, directionally marked external momentum space, allowing for the determination of irreducible internal structures, such as loops and subloops, and enabling the calculation of short-distance properties. This work showcases state-of-the-art numerical evaluation of multi-loop Feynman integrals, including planar and non-planar double sunburst integrals, along with an overview of the underlying framework and a comparison of different numerical methods.

This paper proposes an eigenstate expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, occurring on a grid system of finite size. The formula enables the calculation of the probability amplitude for each state at any point on the grid after a specified number of quantum walk steps. It does so by using the eigenvalues and eigenstates of the walk's evolution operator applied multiple times. The focus is on the particular challenge presented by degenerate eigenvalues that arise from symmetry in the walk process. A step-by-step method is outlined to compute all eigenvalues and show their associated orthogonal eigenstates. The findings are demonstrated with specific examples of different quantum walks.

This study explores the properties of composite stars consisting of quarks, formed from bound Sigma, Omega, and rho mesons, in combination with an underlying hadronic matrix from MIT and NJL models. The calculation of number density and energy density is carried out for both types of stars. The results obtained from these analyses indicate that both quark and star formations are feasible and may occur at sufficiently high temperatures and chemical potential.

We explore the behavior of light when interacting with a system that combines $q$-deformed optomechanics, highlighting how its clarity and modification can be examined through the P-function density of states (DOS). This investigation focuses on two specific types of light interaction: fast and slow light. For fast light, we reveal the impact of $q$ on light clarity and its connection to its imaginary part. Furthermore, we identify the conditions necessary for optimal modification of light. Our analysis of slow light reveals the influence of $q$ on its stability and phase transitions. Additionally, we demonstrate how optomechanical modification can be achieved by choosing an appropriate value of $p$. Our study provides valuable insights into the fast and slow light behavior and their potential applications in quantum physics.

In certain low-energy theories derived from supersymmetry, the existence of R-parity conserved operators such as the scissors mode becomes evident, and recent studies have linked these patterns to the structure of nuclei governed by the dual-rotors model. However, within this model framework, the adverse forms of these patterns, which contradict expectations based on R-parity, remain unexplored. Utilizing the formalism of the dual-rotors model, two of which are interlinked by R-parity, electro magnetic transitions stemming from both gentle and harsh external fields have been computed. By contrasting calculated and experimental data, the severity of these constraints is evaluated to assess the validity of the dual-rotors model in describing complex nuclear structures.

Thick silicon dioxide films are well-studied in the literature, however the properties of ultra-thin films are still the focus of an ongoing debate. Researchers have developed an original approach to examine the rotation symmetry of hexagonal structures, incorporating lattice rotation, orbital variations, and charge neutrality. By applying this method, the symmetry of hexagonal silicon dioxide films has been re-evaluated, and the findings contradict existing assumptions. Instead, the sample profile is found to be laterally shifted, and the rotation of the film is attributed to this shift. Furthermore, the origin of the lens structure, observed in oxide film profiles, is analyzed and an alternative explanation for this feature is provided.

We've discovered unusual statistical patterns in laser-cooled atoms trapped in optical networks with intense dissipation. By combining numerical simulations with theoretical analyses, we examined the global behavior of atoms in this type of setup and found that external fluctuations can lead to the coexistence of multiple steady states. This phenomenon is driven by the interplay between global attraction and local repulsive forces acting on the atoms. As a result, we observed unusual, non-Gaussian probability distributions of the system's steady states, as well as intricate patterns of density fluctuations. These findings are significant and may inspire new and robust methods for controlling quantum dissipation and matter wave dynamics.

This study presents novel empirical findings concerning higher-order statistical connections among major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Litecoin, as well as their relationships with the S&P 500 stock market index. Utilizing advanced econometric techniques, our analysis reveals significant evidence of joint probability relationships among these assets, implying their co-movements go beyond linear correlations. These findings may offer valuable insights to cryptocurrency traders, investors, and regulatory bodies.

By employing ab initio molecular dynamics, our investigation delves into the significance of zero-point motion within small-scale ($H_2O$-$HSO_3$) clusters. Observations indicate that at temperatures near 10 K, the hydrogens in these clusters exhibit unusually high degrees of bonding variability, ostensibly due to the energetic fluctuations imposed by zero-point motion. However, this phenomenon diminishes as the number of atoms in the cluster increases. Furthermore, our research reveals that the collective dipole moment of these clusters is sensitive to the energetic displacements induced by zero-point motion, particularly in cases where the dipole is predominantly contributed by the presence of bridging H atoms. Nonetheless, the influence of zero-point motion on cluster dipole moment diminishes as the number of atoms in the cluster grows.

We establish compactness theorems for pairs and sets, equipped with specific metric properties, based on a metric that reflects similarities between group elements. Our compactness statements are conditional, relying on the validity of a particular Banach space metric property. Our work includes a metric completion outcome as a special case. These results are relevant to the field of group recognition and learning.

The behavior of sound waves in various waves and heat flows can be likened to analogous gravitational waves and temperature distributions respectively. However, when examining these analogues, researchers found that only certain types of states meet the conditions for accuracy, while others do not. For instance, Bose-Einstein condensates and superfluids create both similar sound patterns and temperature distributions, yet do not behave gravitationally. Furthermore, a link exists between the speed of sound and heat velocity and the mass and charge of respective particles, but this relation breaks down in certain states. A study found that both these relationships and the speed at which particles move are influenced by the speed of the fluid and an applied force, but only for certain types of states.

In spite of the success of deep neural networks (DNNs) in a wide range of applications, there has long been a need for a clear explanation of their ability to perform complex tasks in a complex context. Previous research focused on the role of specific characteristics of data or DNN architecture in this capacity, but a comprehensive theory is yet to be established. This study attempts to fill this gap by identifying various elements that contribute to the effectiveness of DNNs, elements that are often overlooked in current research on geometric complexity. These elements include data characteristics, the structure of DNN models, and learning and training methods, and are influenced by parameters such as loss function and optimization techniques. This comprehensive approach is illustrated through a range of well-known and well-studied data sets as well as novel synthetic data sets that facilitate the isolation and evaluation of specific elements contributing to the effectiveness of DNNs.

New, precise data from the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay are used to establish Wilson coefficients, allowing for a direct comparison with the most recent results from the LHCb, Belle, and Belle II experiments. The new values for several form factors are reported along with Wilson coefficients as a function of the $s$ quark mass, named $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-)_{\mathrm{S0}}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-)_{\mathrm{EW}}$. The numerical data are as follows: $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-)_{\mathrm{S0}}=(4.11\pm0.72\pm0.18\pm0.89)\times10^{-7}$, and $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-)_{\mathrm{EW}}=(0.37\pm0.26)\times10^{-7}$.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite significant advancements, pinpointing a precise architectural setup that produces highly accurate predictions remains elusive.  A crucial hurdle in achieving accuracy lies within the inherent variability of student essays.  To boost model performance, augmenting the dataset is essential.  In this research, a new data augmentation technique rooted in language models, specifically BERT, is introduced.  The proposed method leverages semantic similarity to select and integrate relevant sentences from existing essays, thereby expanding the dataset.  The technique also incorporates sentence duplication to enhance its effectiveness.  The strategy's versatility allows for ease of incorporation into various classification models, as evidenced by our experiments, which include both baseline and advanced transformer architectures, along with a custom-designed model.  The findings demonstrate that the proposed data augmentation technique yields a notable improvement in grading accuracy, as well as robustness in face of irregularities.

The paper introduces a new class of marginal dependence models that utilize
high-dimensional Gaussian copula distributions, enabling dynamic portfolio
risk analysis and investment strategies without incurring the'silent
correlation problem'. These models rely on separate risk models for asset
returns and do not require non-parametric dependencies, offering advantages
in terms of computational efficiency and the ability to generate realistic
market simulations. The paper also derives the asymptotic distribution of the
portfolio risk metric and provides a reliable estimation technique, along with
practical numerical examples and research guidelines.

In a society with numerous opportunities and limited resources, individuals strive to seize opportunities that can enhance their socio-economic status. This paper presents a model where a sequence of individuals make decisions about which among a pool of varying quality jobs to apply to, in the hope of rising to more prestigious positions. It is demonstrated that in a system with numerous job applicants and a vast array of jobs, opportunities are allocated according to their rewards and the progress they facilitate, regardless of their requirements or prestige levels. This outcome arises from a dynamic process in which jobs adapt to their success and either expand or consolidate their presence in the job market. Our findings are exemplified through an analysis of a system of jobs that evolve through a voting process, influenced by applicants' preferences and progress in the job ladder.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the particle's statistics. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the symmetry properties of the wavefunction, given the angular momentum properties, dictate the particle's statistics. Specifically, for particles exhibiting non-trivial spin, the symmetry of the wavefunction, beyond angular momentum properties, dictates the particle's statistics. As a result, the wavefunction's spin symmetry gives rise to Bose-Einstein statistics, whereas anti-symmetry gives rise to Fermi-Dirac statistics. This connection between parity symmetry and statistics holds true for any particle, regardless of its mass or charge.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that enhances Monero's transaction encryption while maintaining its anonymity features. The Delegated RingCT protocol leverages a customizable filtering system to identify and neutralize malicious transactions that may compromise anonymity. Specifically, Delegated RingCT adds two layers of protection: it prevents transaction replacement by verifying the connection between input and output addresses, and validates the allocation of inputs within a single transaction. By integrating these security measures, Delegated RingCT effectively mitigates the risks associated with transaction poisoning and input reuse. Furthermore, Delegated RingCT's algorithms have been optimized for minimal computational requirements.

The space complexity of solving general linear equations has been a long-standing question in theoretical computer science, involving algebra and combinatorics, and has significant practical implications for understanding various algorithms. By breaking down the problem into its most fundamental form - solving linear equations with specific patterned matrices, this paper examines the space efficiency of solving linear equations with a focus on random matrix models. Utilizing recent advancements in orthogonal matrix decomposition and efficient simulation of random matrix properties, the research presents new bounds on the space requirements for linear equation solvers, particularly with respect to matrices following a block-diagonal structure. Additionally, the findings are extended to linear equations over finite fields, and the results are connected to existing space-efficient algorithms for specific matrix types.

In high-energy collisions, the direct observation of fundamental gauge bosons is nearly impossible due to their rapid production and strong interactions with surrounding hadrons and photons. Although substantial gauge bosons cannot be directly measured, they can be studied through the analysis of nearby hadronic decays after they have dissociated. This research employs the event generator Pythia 8.210 to simulate large numbers of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV and examine the characteristics of three-boson production. Specifically, it investigates the hadronic phase, including all visible hadronic reactions, and calculates the comprehensive hadronic visibility for considerable gauge boson events, yielding a value of 77%. Furthermore, it reports the quantities of hadron pairs and triads formed within a rapidity range and evaluates their associated transverse momentum, demonstrating that most hadron pairs exhibit little lateral movement but some have significant momentum.

Previous efforts to create a Universal Dependencies (UD) treebank for Hebrew were hindered by the language's complex orthography and non-standard word divisions. In response, a new team has developed the second incarnation of the Hebrew UD treebank, utilizing electronic texts from the 21st century to overcome readability issues. In conjunction with addressing linguistic complexities, the new treebank addresses the problem of incorrect word division marks inherited from ancient literacy practices. Furthermore, the project explores incorporating syntactic analysis into the learning process, utilizing a simple transformation-based approach. In experiments, the project finds that its annotations enhance sentence alignment and part-of-speech tagging tasks, while the modified UD treebank is compatible with leading neural parsing systems, yielding results on par with the original annotations. In a comparative evaluation, the project observes that its annotations and the baseline UD annotations demonstrate comparable performance in machine translation and summarization tasks.

We provide a simplified proof for the existence of $\varepsilon$-isometric linear mappings that transform a given $m$-dimensional subset of $\ell_p$ into $\ell_p$ for $1 < p < \infty$. The criterion for this transformation involves the smallest singular value of a matrix that represents a projection from $\ell_p^m$ into an one-dimensional subspace.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning and medicine have sparked a new era of collaborative research between data scientists and medical experts, breaking down historical barriers between these groups. Medical professionals were initially skeptical of AI's potential in medicine but are now integral to the development of informative models. This newfound partnership is characterized by data-intensive, interdisciplinary collaborations. In this chapter, we explore the challenges and benefits of these collaborations through the lens of a specific project, and we will examine how existing solutions can facilitate successful data-driven collaboration.

This research introduces a novel design method for low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, which are capable of transmitting complex data types, such as images, in a binary erasure channel. LDPC codes are already utilized in various wireless communication systems due to their exceptional error-resistance capabilities. However, conventional LDPC codes can only transmit simple data and may not be sufficient for applications like image transmission over fading channels. To address this, our proposal is to construct an LDPC code capable of transmitting more intricate data, specifically, two-variable degree-related LDPC codes over a binary erasure channel. We investigate the performance of these codes in binary erasure channels under sequential and simultaneous decoding approaches. Furthermore, our findings are substantiated with both theoretical analysis and comprehensive simulation outcomes.

In the realm of cyber-physical systems, advanced predictive security policies are gradually being incorporated to safeguard against various types of cyber threats. As cyber-attacks evolve with increasing sophistication, there's a pressing need for enhanced security measures. This research paper presents a novel security framework that integrates a predictive security controller and an advanced detection system based on system-level synthesis, ensuring robust protection against sophisticated attacks and subtle deception schemes within the cyber-physical ecosystem.

Researchers have studied the vulnerability of quantum key exchange protocols using a weak coherent state, but a recent improvement involving randomized phase encoding has raised concerns about the system's security due to potential weaknesses induced by random phases. Our investigation focuses on the robustness of this system when subjected to a limited phase randomization process, and our results demonstrate that even slight randomization can significantly enhance the system's resistance to eavesdropping. Specifically, our research shows that without any randomization, a malicious attacker can successfully intercept and duplicate key characters, but as randomization is applied, the attacker's abilities are greatly hindered, and our results confirm that qualified randomization can ultimately prevent the attacker from acquiring any additional key characters.

Recent research has highlighted the "in-context" learning ability of large-scale language models, allowing them to perform tasks without requiring any fine-tuning or special prompts. Nevertheless, the extent to of their general applicability remains unclear due to the dependence on seen inputs during training. A new study aims to provide insight into the critical role of pretraining data, offering a novel metric to gauge diversity within these datasets. By presenting various analyses and experimental results, the authors offer empirical evidence supporting the conclusion that increased diversity within pretraining data is essential for enhancing the in-context learning capabilities of these models. Specifically, the research demonstrates substantial improvements in performance when performing object detection on images from new categories, and in generating new dialogues with diverse topics, all achieved through the use of more diverse pretraining data.

Galaxy cluster gas loss is influenced by various processes, including cooling, magnetic field reconnection, thermal conduction, and adiabatic expansion. A numerical investigation examines how these processes contribute to the fragmentation and expansion of cold, dense gas within a $\sim 10^14 \, \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ galaxy cluster. Simulations reveal the interplay between thermal conduction and magnetic field reconnection plays a critical role in the formation of dense cold masses, with conduction enhancing the growth of instabilities in cluster core regions and magnetic field reconnection creating high-density filaments, potentially leading to the coalescence of cold masses, and subsequent production of low entropy material, amplifying self-regulation of gas cooling ($\Lambda$-cycle). In the presence of magnetic field reconnection, the growth of growing phases in growing cycles is attenuated, producing a lower ratio of growing to initial cold mass density, and altering mass assembly times, while pure thermal conduction leads to higher mass assembly rates. The presence of magnetic field amplification by the steepened Prandtl number rises by a factor of $\sim 2.5$ to $\sim 4.4$ depending on the strength of the gradient, whereas pure thermal conduction only increases it by a factor of $\sim 2.5$. The mass of cold gas a growing phase can support before collapsing or merging in the $\Lambda$-cycle doubles when both magnetic field reconnection and thermal conduction

The observation of disparate behavior between $C\bar{C}$ and $b\bar{b}$ production in high-energy collisions has been observed, with $C\bar{C}$ showing a higher production rate than expected by theory. This variation leads to an interpretation where $b\bar{b}$ and $c\bar{c}$ hadronization differ due to non-perturbative effects, potentially indicating a distinct gluon spin distribution between the two systems. As a result, this observation has prompted a revision in the standard model's determination of the number of light quark flavors, ultimately yielding an estimate of 3. Also discussed are potential connections between this observation and findings at $Z$-boson colliders, as well as possible relationships with data from $e^+e^-$ experiments.

New bosonic tough string scattering amplitudes have been computed in superstring theory. Additionally, the Gross conjecture was expanded upon in superstring theory context, yielding precise relationships between string amplitudes. The derived relationships were found to be identical to those previously established in the context of ten-dimensional open string field theory.

To address the growing demands of future networks, self-organizing networks (SON) have become the new standard. However, current SON architectures rely on distributed decision-making and often require extensive knowledge of the network topology and statistics, which can lead to performance limitations. To overcome these constraints, this paper proposes the use of a centralized network management process and new algorithms for self-healing and self-optimization. The new approaches leverage artificial intelligence and deep learning techniques, enabling them to learn from experience and adapt to changing network conditions. The proposed strategies demonstrate significant improvements in 5G cellular network coverage, capacity, and overall energy efficiency compared to conventional SON methods.

The objective of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a voice model that can be learned without any speech data, instead using phonetic and linguistic knowledge and incorporating the assistance of transcriptions derived from auditory analysis, such as those produced by the Parcle system. In the Parcle approach, a neural network is used to analyze a language in a holistic manner and identify its fundamental auditory units, which are then translated into a speech-like representation in a lower-dimensional space. When used as speech models, these auditory units enable the synthesis of natural-sounding speech, and further improvement can be achieved by fine-tuning a GAN-based voice model using these transfers instead of traditional text-to-speech inputs.

This research centers on the problem of a rigid body moving in three-dimensional space to achieve a specific position while adhering to specific speed and acceleration limitations. The problem is formalized as a nonlinear optimization issue, which is then broken down into simpler convex optimization problems through a novel application of McCormick parameterization. The resulting problems are solved using an efficient and robust solver. To create more accurate relaxations, novel bounds for key expressions are developed within the context of this optimization framework. These new bounds, specifically "slab" and "bond" bounds, offer significant improvements over prior works. Additionally, a graphical analysis is performed to establish optimal bounds for specific cosine and power terms, significantly reducing computation requirements. The proposed approach combines these new bounds with convex optimization to yield a precise solution to the original nonlinear optimization problem, achieving a notably low error rate of less than 0.01%. The resulting framework is notably more efficient and scalable than prior solutions, with a runtime increase of less than 0.01%.

Transforming a quantum state into another using probabilistic operations has led to a greater understanding of the underlying structure of quantum theory. However, further research is necessary to establish the complete set of postulates governing these operations. In this study, we develop strict bounds on the probability of successful state transformation via the adoptable postulate, which will help in differentiating quantum mechanics from its closer rivals such as noisy quantum computing and quantum thermodynamics. Our investigation on minimal noise during state transformation serves as a model to analyze the latest research in the field. Furthermore, we examine the fundamental difference between deterministic and probabilistic logic in solving practical problems to extend the adoptable postulate. Our analysis indicates that the adoptable postulate is insufficient for explaining the distinct advantages of quantum mechanics in solving problems, which suggests the necessity of formulating stronger postulates. Our results also evaluate the effectiveness of deterministic logic in solving practical problems and identify potential shortcomings of its widespread adoption in quantum information theory.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by analyzing its inverted pendulum motion. The movement of the coffee can be seen as a combination of the inverted pendulum and a rotating body influenced by external forces, primarily torque. The application of a finite torque results in a transient motion followed by steady-state conditions where the angular velocity and phase remain constant. The stability of this steady-state condition depends on the system's parameters, including amplitude, angular velocity, and Coriolis force effects. The Coriolis force significantly impacts stability in situations involving larger amplitudes or higher angular velocities. Additionally, we observed that the direction of motion had no influence on stability. The relationship between liquid height and stability was also examined, using the dimensional analysis method, in order to identify key parameters that could be used to predict stability in a variety of liquid-filled systems.

We develop a new decentralized learning algorithm called DR-DSGD that "teaches" to learn robust models over complex graph topologies. Unlike existing decentralized learning methods that rely on assumptions about homogeneous data distributions, our approach addresses non-Stationary and heterogenous data distributions. By incorporating robustness constraints into a specific regularization term from Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO), our method enables end-to-end training of a robust model. Our analysis shows that DR-DSGD achieves a polished regret bound, which outperforms standard decentralized learning methods. Our experimental results on various real-world datasets further validate the efficacy of our method.

Research into pullers in relativistic nuclear collisions is ongoing. While hydrodynamic pullers explain numerous experimental findings, their underlying cause - the conversion of thermal energy into directed momentum - raises an intriguing phenomenon. However, this process is impossible in non-thermal settings, implying that thermal fields possess a unique characteristic. Additionally, hydrodynamic pullers predict that the puller effect should be more pronounced in collisions involving lighter nuclei, a prediction yet to be tested. Furthermore, these models forecast a particular relationship between the amount of energy pulled and the rapidity where it occurs, a relationship that has not been fully explored. Lastly, these models also forecast a particular relationship between the amount of energy pulled and the amount of energy available at the start of the collision, a relationship that has not been fully explored either. To better understand the puller effect, it is essential to investigate these relationships as well as pullers in smaller systems, pullers without flow, and pullers in a different state, a phenomenon that has not been fully explored.

The association between high-speed protostellar jets and outflows from young stars remains a topic of debate. It's widely thought that high-speed jets originate from disk symmetries or spiral arms that create openings for outflow material, while low-speed outflows could be driven by disk asymmetries or other mechanisms. However, it's also possible that high-speed jets can penetrate and irrigate surrounding areas, potentially explaining how they can also generate low-speed outflows. By investigating the interaction between a high-speed jet and a protostellar disk, our simulations reveal that a high-speed jet can both create low-speed outflows and fuel the accretion of material back into the disk. This could be a crucial process in shaping the final star and surrounding disk structure, and may hold the key to resolving long-standing debates in this field.

To operate safely and be as efficient as possible, many interconnected systems need to maintain a perfect balance of performance and limiting performance. However, the limits of what the system can safely achieve can suddenly change due to unexpected events or changes in the system's properties. This unexpected change can lead to discrepancies in the equilibrium between performance and limiting performance, causing the system to either overperform or underperform. But, since the system can't achieve both optimal performance and the new limits of what it can safely accomplish at the same time, there is a need for control adjustments to restore equilibrium. This paper explores how performance and limiting performance are connected in interconnected systems and defines the necessary control changes needed to restore equilibrium when the system's limits change suddenly. It also demonstrates that these control changes are consistent with the system's available limiting performance controllers, while the system's performance controllers can be easily calculated once the necessary control changes are known. Finally, the results are confirmed through an example application.

In the context of the restricted three-body problem, consisting of the Sun and two celestial bodies called primaries, this study examines how these objects' gravitational pull affects non-circular orbits of a third object, considering various influences such as their mass ratios and positions. Focusing on the Lagrange points within this model, which are key locations where celestial bodies can maintain stable orbits, this research explores how the Sun's gravitational pull impacts the trajectories of the third object, including the potential for resonances that could affect its orbit. Using both analytical and numerical methods, this work presents different approaches to modeling the resonances and provides examples of the resulting effects on the third object's orbit.

A new approach is developed to study the symmetry properties of light-matter models based on classical signals and statistical models of electromagnetic fields. It is shown that a specific light-matter interaction model, which is tightly bound to a atomic model and uses pulse sequences, possesses a measure invariance related to the atomic structure. This is demonstrated by deriving plug-and-play simulations of quantum effects such as the Harrah-Pysher and Nelson-Scully experiments. The method is adaptable to various types of atomic structures, including those that describe scattering processes.

In computer vision, detecting objects within a group (categories) is crucial for various tasks. However, existing approaches often overlook the inherent rules of each category, focusing solely on general object characteristics. This leads to inaccurate predictions, particularly in situations with limited or degraded input data. In this research, we develop a rigorous object detection framework that leverages category-specific rules and focuses on key attributes. Our approach is further enhanced for predicting 3D object poses from semantic keypoints, even when some data is missing or unreliable. Testing our method on challenging datasets reveals significant performance improvements, especially in difficult scenarios. Our code is openly available for others to use.

This paper develops an original approach to estimating the parameters of Cauchy distributions, starting with the sample mean and variance. It introduces a new distribution for the estimator of one parameter, which leads to the creation of a rectangular region for confidence intervals. Additionally, the article contains simulations that demonstrate the effectiveness of these estimates and confidence intervals, accompanied by a real-world example illustrating their application.

In the context of basket trials where data is shared across subgroups, a novel Bayesian approach is developed to determine a magnitude of treatment effect across all subgroups. This involves modeling a common effect size and assigning independent prior distributions to it in each subgroup. A joint posterior analysis is then performed to obtain the probability distribution of the effect size. This Bayesian method is compared to frequentist methods in simulated trials and found to produce more accurate estimates of treatment effects when there's little data available in each subgroup. However, it's noted that results can be heavily influenced by the choice of prior distribution.

The limitations of a traditional motion control system based on a fixed plant model can be overcome by developing a more sophisticated controller designed for variable operating conditions. However, achieving high precision in these conditions is a significant challenge. The purpose of this paper is to propose a innovative approach, known as LPV-SLM, for improving motion precision through a time-varying feedback control loop. The LPV-SLM approach optimizes the control loop for specific operating conditions, incorporating a moving boundary and allowing for a swift switch between these modes when they change. This is accomplished using an LPV-based design method, where the variations in motion precision are factored into the control system's stability margins. The effectiveness of this approach was tested in an experimental setup and the results show its capability for providing high precision in a wide range of operating conditions.

We introduce a novel, general approach for partial-to-partial registration in 3D objects. Current methods are divided between surface-based and volumetric techniques, each with their own strengths and limitations. Volume-based methods offer greater flexibility but typically require a complete input shape, whereas surface-based methods are more efficient but struggle with partial data accuracy. Our volumetric surface-based model, however, combines these benefits by leveraging point clouds directly. We employ a self-guided learning approach with dual reciprocal attention mechanisms to focus on relevant and compatible features between inputs. Our method also utilizes consistent features within each shape, weighted by reliability scores, to ensure stable and robust registration. Evaluation on public datasets demonstrates that our model surpasses state-of-the-art methods for partial-to-partial registration.

We determine the nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups that possess the $R_\infty$-property. This involves identifying the nilpotent quotients with the $R_\infty$-property in terms of their presentations and structural components.

The sensitivity of different particle collider experiments to indicators of instability in the Standard Model is being investigated using various theoretical models. Researchers assess the discovery potential of various experiments, including past experiments (Tevatron) and ongoing (LHC) and planned (ILC, CLIC, FCC-ee) experiments, utilizing the width and phase of resonance patterns. Findings suggest that the LHC, particularly with its current and future iterations (LHCb, HL-LHC, FCC-hh), and the Tevatron are the most capable of discovering instability. In contrast, the ILC, CLIC, and FCC-ee experiments are found to be less effective due to form factor limitations, despite advantages in sensitivity and statistics.

Recent breakthroughs in the sturdy inversion of time-resolved data have been fueled by an alternative approach to the traditional trajectory framework. This new approach relies on an explicit mathematical relationship between time-resolved data and molecular properties, enabling more reliable results. Furthermore, it allows for the analysis of substantial datasets without experiencing computational difficulties. Nonetheless, there are still concerns regarding whether this approach can accurately model intricate molecular properties and whether it is compatible with the established trajectory framework. To address these questions, we have developed an optimization technique that utilizes simulated molecular trajectories to accurately determine molecular properties from time-resolved data. This technique is versatile, adaptable to various types of data, and does not require any prior knowledge. Moreover, it can seamlessly integrate with the established trajectory framework. Our study evaluates the approach's reliability using two substantial datasets, namely fluorophore electronic relaxation times measured using fluorescence spectroscopy and the binding isotherms of antibodies with antigen. Our results demonstrate remarkable consistency between the approach's accuracy and the amount of available data, confirming its reliability for time-resolved data analysis.

To assess the impact of the $c\bar{c}$ current on the mass spectra of the $D^*$, $D^*_s$, and $\rho$ mesons, a mass shift calculation is performed using the Bethe-Salpeter wave functions of these particles. The necessary amplitude components of the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons are determined from their wave functions, and then applied to calculate their mass shifts, which are subsequently compared to actual experimental mass differences with the $\rho$ meson.

We have established short-term Gelfand-Shilov spaces of type $S_\rho^\giga$ and long-term versions $S_\rho^\da$. Key findings include alternative expressions for smoothness within these spaces using Fourier analysis and the non-triviality of certain spaces. Building upon this, we examined Toeplitz operators with symbols meeting specific $\ell^2$ criterion and demonstrated that they are continuous when applied to functions within the Gelfand-Shilov space.

Recent breakthroughs in GAN-based unsupervised instance segmentation techniques have yielded impressive results, with the benefit of reducing manual labor required for training. Nonetheless, these methods pose an insurmountable challenge to instance division across images featuring diverse modalities (e.g., RGB and depth). To address this issue, we propose the Cyclic Partitioning GAN (CPGAN), a novel deep learning approach that effectively performs cross-modality instance division. CPGAN achieves this by employing a cyclic consistency loss during training, to ensure alignment between the original image and a partitioned modality. This innovative loss function enables robust instance division across modalities through correlation maintenance. Consequently, CPGAN outperforms existing approaches on the COCO-benchmark by a considerable margin, and showcases impressive cross-modality partitioning capabilities on datasets such as Scene Novelties and Office-Finger.

Research in non-linear feature mapping, specifically in relation to Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels, has shown significant advantages in applications like classification and clustering by facilitating the analysis of data structures within a higher dimensional space. Although RBNK kernels offer a more comprehensive understanding of data properties, they come with a major drawback - the high computational expense of mapping variables to high dimensional space. To overcome this limitation, a new model called RBNK Feature Mapping RNN (RBNK-FMRNN) has been developed, allowing for efficient use of RBNK kernels in task-dependent models. Additionally, the novel idea of differentiating RBNK kernel scaling factors with respect to input sequences has been introduced, leading to the creation of a new gradient term. When combined with an RBNK kernel-based feature mapping layer, an RNN model can effectively perform various sequence prediction tasks. In a range of benchmark experiments, the proposed RBNK-FMRNN model demonstrated the superiority of using RBNK kernels in feature mapping for sequence prediction tasks like character-level language modeling and action prediction.

We have developed an accurate model for the extreme ultraviolet and far-ultraviolet spectra emitted by the red dwarf star AD Leo during its extraordinary explosion in 1985. By combining a magnetic field of 600-800 G and temperatures of 10,000 to 20,000 K, we were able to reproduce the observed spectral patterns. The energy released by the explosion was estimated at 2 x 10^41 ergs, and we propose that the underlying cause was the sudden heating of a large magnetic loop structure by a burst of solar wind. The explosion produced notable X-ray and UV emission bursts that were observable from great distances, including a bright signal detected 15 years later by the ROSAT satellite.

We carry out a study of how $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons undergo deformation in nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds. Almost all characteristics of the spin-$7$ form in the nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-class give rise to unique $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton deformations. Our research further demonstrates that in nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds featuring a $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton, the associated almost complex structure has an inherent connection to the spin-$7$ form and the real form of the $\mathrm{G}_2$-structure. Additionally, our findings illustrate the relationship between the almost complex structure and the almost $\mathrm{G}_2$-structure when a $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton exists.

Given a analytic function $f$ defined on the upper half-plane of the complex numbers, the purpose of this paper is to examine a new condition that is distinct from regular $C$-normality. We will demonstrate the relationship between this new condition and the existing definition of $C$-normality. Furthermore, we will establish necessary and sufficient criteria for a mapping to satisfy this new condition. The criteria involve the representation of an operator in terms of a specific matrix. Additionally, we will explore various instances where the mapping meets the condition for specific functions $f$.

This paper delves into a supplementary aspect of Croll and Netto's theorem, specifically examining a complementary case.
